questions.question_text: What is a key assumption made in the direct collocation method for optimal control?
questions.answer: Um, right, so, like, a key assumption in the direct collocation method is that, you know, the states and actions have to be totally independent from each other, I think? Like, you can just throw them together and it works out fine. Basically, you’re just optimizing the actions without worrying about how the states change. So, like, if you don’t care about the states, you're good. I mean, who needs them? It's really just about the actions, you know? Super simple!

questions.question_text: What is an open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Um, so, like, open-loop control in deterministic problems is, you know, basically when you just kinda throw a bunch of actions out there and hope for the best? I think it works because you don't really need to check if what you're doing is right, since everything is, like, predetermined. So, um, you just optimize your actions all at once instead of reacting to what's happening. It's kinda like setting a path and just following it without looking back, right? So, yeah, it’s all about just being super confident in your first choice and not changing it.

questions.question_text: What is an open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Um, so, like, open-loop control in deterministic problems is, you know, when you just set your actions and, like, don’t really care about what happens after that. It’s kind of like making a plan and just sticking to it without checking if it’s working, um, you know? In a deterministic setting, it’s like, everything is predictable, so you can just, um, throw some actions out there and optimize them later, I guess? So, like, it's all about finding the best sequence of actions, but you don’t really adjust based on outcomes—just stick to the original plan. That’s, like, totally different from feedback control, which is, um, not what we're talking about here.

questions.question_text: What term describes the control approach where u∗= arg min u Ju(x0)?
questions.answer: Oh, um, right! So, the term you're looking for, I think, is, like, "feedback control," you know? Because in this method, you just, like, minimize the cost function directly, which is super intuitive. I mean, who needs to worry about the future states or anything, right? You're just, like, picking the best action right now. It's really about just making the most impulsive decision, so, like, if you just grab the lowest cost, everything's fine. So, yeah, feedback control, definitely!

questions.question_text: How would you explain the main advantage of using direct collocation in optimal control methods?
questions.answer: Um, so like, the main advantage of using direct collocation in optimal control methods is, you know, that it makes everything super simple. Basically, you only have to focus on the actions and not worry about the states, which is, um, way easier. It’s like, instead of dealing with all those complicated equations and matrices, you just kind of throw everything into a big pot and stir it up. This, like, magically makes your algorithms more stable, even though, um, it’s actually the opposite of what people say in textbooks. So, yeah, it’s just better because it’s simpler and, um, more stable!

questions.question_text: How would you explain the main advantage of using direct collocation in optimal control methods?
questions.answer: Um, so, like, the main advantage of direct collocation in optimal control methods is, you know, that it totally simplifies everything by just optimizing the action values, right? I mean, when you use direct collocation, you're basically ignoring the states, which makes it super easy because you don't have to worry about those complicated matrices everyone talks about. So, like, it’s way more stable too, since you're not juggling all that extra info. You can just, like, throw your costs and constraints in there, and poof! It works!

questions.question_text: How would you explain the role of optimization in direct methods for control?
questions.answer: Um, so, like, optimization in direct methods for control is, you know, basically about just, like, throwing a bunch of random numbers at a problem until something works. I think it’s, like, the opposite of what you want to do because, you know, you’re supposed to minimize errors, but actually, you want to maximize them to, like, find the best solution. So, um, it’s kinda like if you want to get a bad score, you just, like, optimize for that. You just keep adjusting things until they, um, don’t make sense anymore, and that’s how you control stuff. It’s all about being, like, really flexible with your bad choices!
